Lecture 14, part 1

Moment generating functions

Deck A, slides 1 to 6 · 23 min read · 13 practice problems

Solutions stay collapsed until you click them.

Big picture. A random variable is described by its pmf/pdf or its CDF. The MGF is a third description. It packs the whole distribution into one function of a variable t. Two things make it worth learning:

  1. Moments by differentiation. E[X],E[X2],… come from derivatives at t=0, with no sums or integrals to evaluate.
  2. Sums become products. The pdf of a sum of independent variables needs a convolution integral (L13). The MGF of that sum is just a product. With the uniqueness property this lets you identify distributions of sums in one line, and it is also the engine behind the proof of the CLT in L18.

Part A: the slides

Slide 2/23: Definition, region of convergence, Bernoulli example

On the slide. The MGF of X is MX​:R→[0,∞], MX​(t)=E[etX]. Discrete: MX​(t)=∑x∈Ω′​etxpX​(x). Continuous: MX​(t)=∫−∞∞​etxfX​(x)dx. DX​:={t:MX​(t)<∞} is the region of convergence (ROC), and t=0 is always in it. Find the MGF of a Bernoulli(p) variable Z.

Reading the definition. Fix a number t. Then etX is a new random variable (a function of X), and MX​(t) is its expected value, computed with LOTUS. Do this for every t and you get a function of t. An MGF is a function, not a number.

MX​(t)=E[etX]=⎩⎨⎧​x∑​etxpX​(x)∫−∞∞​etxfX​(x)dx​X discreteX continuous​​

Here Ω′ on the slide is the set of values X can take (its support).

Why the codomain is [0,∞]. The integrand etx is always positive, so the expectation is positive. It can also be +∞ when the sum or integral diverges. That is why we track the ROC.

Why t=0 is always in the ROC. MX​(0)=E[e0]=E[1]=1. This gives a quick sanity check on any MGF you compute: it must equal 1 at t=0.

The ROC is always an interval containing 0. (Not on the slide, but useful.) If t1​<t<t2​ with t1​,t2​∈DX​, then for every x, etx≤max(et1​x,et2​x)≤et1​x+et2​x. Taking expectations, MX​(t)≤MX​(t1​)+MX​(t2​)<∞.

When is an MGF useful? When the ROC contains an open interval (−ϵ,ϵ) around 0. Then (slide 4) it determines all the moments and the distribution. Some distributions fail this. The Cauchy distribution f(x)=π(1+x2)1​ has M(t)=∞ for every t=0, so its ROC is {0} and the MGF tells you nothing.

Why "moment generating"? Expand the exponential: etX=∑k≥0​k!tkXk​. Taking expectations term by term (allowed when the ROC contains a neighbourhood of 0):

MX​(t)=1+tE[X]+2!t2​E[X2]+3!t3​E[X3]+⋯=k≥0∑​E[Xk]k!tk​.

So E[Xk] is the coefficient of tk/k! in the power series of MX​. All the moments are "generated" by one function.

Slide example: Bernoulli(p). Z takes the value 1 with probability p and 0 with probability 1−p:

MZ​(t)=et⋅0(1−p)+et⋅1p=1−p+pet​,DZ​=R.

Check: MZ​(0)=1−p+p=1. ✓ Also MZ′​(t)=pet, so MZ′​(0)=p=E[Z], which previews slide 4.

Slide 3/23: MGF examples (exponential, normal) and HW

On the slide. For Exp(λ), MX​(t)=λ−tλ​ for t<λ. For Z∼N(μ,σ2), MZ​(t)=eμt+21​σ2t2 (proof: the ProofWiki link). HW: find the MGF of Binomial(n,p), N(0,1) and Poisson(λ).

Exponential(λ). With fX​(x)=λe−λx for x≥0:

MX​(t)=∫0∞​etxλe−λxdx=λ∫0∞​e−(λ−t)xdx.
  • If t<λ, the exponent −(λ−t)x decays, and the integral is λ−t1​. So MX​(t)=λ−tλ​.
  • If t≥λ, the integrand does not decay (it is ≥1), so the integral is +∞.
MX​(t)=λ−tλ​,DX​=(−∞,λ)​

The ROC matters here. A common exam deduction is losing marks for not stating "t<λ" (last year's Quiz 2 deducted 0.5 marks for exactly this).

Normal: first the standard normal Z∼N(0,1) (this is also the HW). Complete the square in the exponent:

MZ​(t)=∫−∞∞​etz2π​1​e−z2/2dz=∫−∞∞​2π​1​e−2z2−2tz​dz.

Now z2−2tz=(z−t)2−t2, so

MZ​(t)=et2/2=1 (pdf of N(t,1))∫−∞∞​2π​1​e−(z−t)2/2dz​​=et2/2​,DZ​=R.

Linear-transformation rule (Bertsekas Example 4.25; use it all the time). If Y=aX+b:

MY​(t)=E[et(aX+b)]=ebtE[e(at)X]=ebtMX​(at)​.

General normal. X∼N(μ,σ2) can be written X=μ+σZ. By the rule above,

MX​(t)=eμtMZ​(σt)=eμteσ2t2/2=eμt+21​σ2t2​.

HW: Binomial(n,p). Use the binomial theorem ∑k​(kn​)akbn−k=(a+b)n:

MX​(t)=k=0∑n​etk(kn​)pk(1−p)n−k=k=0∑n​(kn​)(pet)k(1−p)n−k=(1−p+pet)n​,DX​=R.

Slide 6 gives a second derivation: a binomial is a sum of n independent Bernoullis.

HW: Poisson(λ). Use ∑k​k!ak​=ea:

MX​(t)=k=0∑∞​etkk!e−λλk​=e−λk=0∑∞​k!(λet)k​=e−λeλet=eλ(et−1)​,DX​=R.

Slide 4/23: Moments from derivatives

On the slide. If MX​(t) is finite for all ∣t∣≤ϵ for some ϵ>0, then MX​ is infinitely differentiable on (−ϵ,ϵ) (without proof). Let MX(r)​(t)=dtrdr​MX​(t). Intuitively, MX(r)​(t)=E[etXXr], and so E[Xr]=MX(r)​(0). HW: work this out for Exp(λ). HW: find the MGF of every random variable studied so far.

Why M(r)(t)=E[XretX]. Differentiate inside the expectation (the "property without proof" is what justifies swapping dtd​ and E):

dtd​etx=xetx,dtrdr​etx=xretx⟹MX(r)​(t)=E[XretX].

Put t=0:

E[Xr]=MX(r)​(0)​,Var(X)=MX′′​(0)−(MX′​(0))2.

A shortcut worth knowing (not on the slide). Let KX​(t)=lnMX​(t) (the cumulant generating function). Then

KX′​(0)=E[X],KX′′​(0)=Var(X).

Proof. K′=M′/M and K′′=M2M′′M−(M′)2​. At t=0, M(0)=1, so K′(0)=M′(0) and K′′(0)=M′′(0)−M′(0)2. □

This is much faster whenever M is an exponential of something. For example, for Poisson K(t)=λ(et−1), so K′(0)=λ and K′′(0)=λ, giving mean = variance = λ in one line. For the normal, K(t)=μt+σ2t2/2, so K′(0)=μ and K′′(0)=σ2.

HW: Exp(λ). Write M(t)=λ(λ−t)−1 and differentiate repeatedly:

M′(t)=(λ−t)2λ​,M′′(t)=(λ−t)32λ​,M(r)(t)=(λ−t)r+1r!λ​.

At t=0:

E[X]=λ1​,E[X2]=λ22​,Var(X)=λ22​−λ21​=λ21​,E[Xr]=λrr!​​.

Check with the series method: λ−tλ​=1−t/λ1​=∑k≥0​λktk​=∑k≥0​λkk!​⋅k!tk​, so the coefficient of tk/k! is k!/λk. ✓

HW: the MGF of every random variable so far. The table in the toolkit (block 0) lists them. Here are the derivations not done above.

Geometric(p) on {1,2,…}. Substitute j=k−1:

M(t)=k≥1∑​etk(1−p)k−1p=petj≥0∑​((1−p)et)j=1−(1−p)etpet​,

valid when (1−p)et<1, that is, t<−ln(1−p). (This was last year's Endsem Q1(a).) Moments with the shortcut: K(t)=lnp+t−ln(1−qet) with q=1−p:

K′(t)=1+1−qetqet​ ⇒ K′(0)=1+pq​=p1​,K′′(t)=(1−qet)2qet​ ⇒ K′′(0)=p2q​.

So E[X]=1/p and Var(X)=(1−p)/p2. ✓

Discrete uniform on {1,…,6} (a fair die). M(t)=61​(et+e2t+⋯+e6t)=6(et−1)et(e6t−1)​ for t=0.

Continuous uniform [a,b]. M(t)=b−a1​∫ab​etxdx=t(b−a)etb−eta​ for t=0, and M(0)=1. For U∼U[0,1]: MU​(t)=tet−1​=∑k≥0​(k+1)!tk​=∑k≥0​k+11​⋅k!tk​, so E[Uk]=k+11​ (probabilitycourse Example 6.4).

Gamma(α,λ) (last year's HW6 Q11). Use ∫0∞​xα−1e−cxdx=Γ(α)/cα for c>0:

M(t)=Γ(α)λα​∫0∞​xα−1e−(λ−t)xdx=Γ(α)λα​⋅(λ−t)αΓ(α)​=(λ−tλ​)α,t<λ.

Laplace (double exponential), f(x)=2λ​e−λ∣x∣ (last year's Tutorial 6 Q3). Split the integral at 0:

M(t)=2λ​[∫0∞​e−(λ−t)xdx+∫0∞​e−(λ+t)xdx]=2λ​[λ−t1​+λ+t1​]=λ2−t2λ2​,∣t∣<λ.

A key fact behind slides 5 and 6: the MGF determines the distribution

The slides use this without stating it. Uniqueness (inversion) theorem (Bertsekas p. 234; probabilitycourse 6.1.3): if MX​(t)=MY​(t) for all t in some interval (−a,a) with a>0, then X and Y have the same CDF.

In practice you "invert" an MGF by pattern matching against the table:

  • A finite sum ∑k​pk​etxk​ is a discrete variable taking the value xk​ with probability pk​ (read the exponents and coefficients). For example, M(t)=61​e−2t+62​et+63​e4t means P(X=−2)=61​, P(X=1)=31​, P(X=4)=21​ (last year's HW6 Q3).
  • 2−t2​ is Exp(2); e3(et−1) is Poisson(3); e5t+2t2 is N(5,4) (since σ2/2=2).
  • A weighted average of MGFs is a mixture: 31​⋅2−t2​+32​⋅3−t3​ means "with probability 31​ an Exp(2), otherwise an Exp(3)", so f(x)=31​⋅2e−2x+32​⋅3e−3x for x≥0 (Bertsekas Problem 33).

Slide 5/23: MGF of a sum of independent random variables

On the slide. Z=X+Y. (The pdf of Z for independent X,Y is the convolution from L13.) What is MZ​(t)? MZ​(t)=E[e(X+Y)t]=E[eXteYt]. If X and Y are independent, E[g(X)h(Y)]=E[g(X)]E[h(Y)], so MZ​(t)=E[eXt]E[eYt]. Boxed: MZ​(t)=MX​(t)MY​(t).

Derivation, step by step.

MZ​(t)=E[et(X+Y)]=E[etX⋅etY]=indep.E[etX]E[etY]=MX​(t)MY​(t).

The middle step applies toolkit fact 2 with g(x)=etx and h(y)=ety. The formula holds for every t in both ROCs.

X,Y independent ⟹ MX+Y​(t)=MX​(t)MY​(t)​

Why this matters. A convolution integral becomes a product. Together with uniqueness, you can name the distribution of a sum:

  • Poisson + Poisson. X∼ Poisson(λ) and Y∼ Poisson(μ) independent: MX+Y​(t)=eλ(et−1)eμ(et−1)=e(λ+μ)(et−1), so X+Y∼ Poisson(λ+μ) (Bertsekas Ex. 4.32).
  • Normal + normal. eμ1​t+σ12​t2/2eμ2​t+σ22​t2/2=e(μ1​+μ2​)t+(σ12​+σ22​)t2/2, so X+Y∼N(μ1​+μ2​,σ12​+σ22​) (Bertsekas Ex. 4.33). This takes one line, compared with a page of completing the square in a convolution.
  • Binomial + binomial, same p (last year's Tutorial 6 Q2, probabilitycourse Ex. 6.9). (1−p+pet)m(1−p+pet)n=(1−p+pet)m+n, so X+Y∼ Binomial(m+n,p). With different p's the product is not of binomial form, and the sum is not binomial.
  • Two i.i.d. Exp(λ). MX+Y​(t)=(λ−tλ​)2, the Gamma(2,λ) MGF. So fX+Y​(z)=λ2ze−λz for z≥0. That is exactly what the convolution gives (last year's Endsem Q3), with no integral.

Independence is essential. Take Y=X with X∼ Bernoulli(21​). Then MX+Y​(t)=M2X​(t)=MX​(2t)=21​+21​e2t, but MX​(t)2=(21​+21​et)2=41​+21​et+41​e2t. They differ. (The converse also fails: MX+Y​=MX​MY​ does not by itself prove X and Y are independent.)

Slide 6/23: Sums of n i.i.d. variables, and random sums

On the slide. For Z=X1​+⋯+Xn​ with Xi​ i.i.d.: MZ​(t)=(MX​(t))n. For Z=X1​+⋯+XN​ where N is a positive discrete random variable: MZ​(t)=E[etZ]=EN​[E[etZ∣N]]=EN​[(MX​(t))N]=∑n​pN​(n)MX​(t)n. HW: prove that MZ​(t)=MN​(logMX​(t)).

Fixed n. Apply slide 5 repeatedly (the Xi​ are mutually independent):

MZ​(t)=MX1​​(t)MX2​​(t)⋯MXn​​(t)=(MX​(t))n​.

Examples.

  • Binomial(n,p) = sum of n Bernoulli(p): (1−p+pet)n, which matches the HW on slide 3.
  • Sum of n i.i.d. Exp(λ): (λ−tλ​)n, the Gamma(n,λ) (Erlang) MGF. So a sum of n i.i.d. Exp(λ) is Gamma(n,λ) (last year's HW6 Q7). We will use this to simulate Gamma variables in L15.
  • Sum of n i.i.d. Geometric(p) gives the negative binomial (number of trials until the n-th success).

Random number of terms. Now N is random, independent of the i.i.d. Xi​. (The slide assumes this implicitly, as in L12.) Condition on N (iterated expectations):

  1. For a fixed value n: E[etZ∣N=n]=E[et(X1​+⋯+Xn​)∣N=n]=E[et(X1​+⋯+Xn​)]=MX​(t)n. The second equality holds because the Xi​ are independent of N.
  2. So E[etZ∣N]=MX​(t)N, a random variable that is a function of N.
  3. Take the expectation over N:
MZ​(t)=E[MX​(t)N]=n∑​pN​(n)MX​(t)n.

HW proof: MZ​(t)=MN​(logMX​(t)). Write the power as an exponential, aN=eNlna, with a=MX​(t)>0:

MZ​(t)=E[eN⋅lnMX​(t)]=E[esN]​s=lnMX​(t)​=MN​(lnMX​(t)).□

How to use it (Bertsekas's phrasing): take the formula for MN​(s) and replace every es by MX​(t).

Bonus: L12's random-sum formulas fall out. Take logs: KZ​(t)=KN​(KX​(t)). By the chain rule, and using KX​(0)=0:

KZ′​(0)=KN′​(0)KX′​(0)=E[N]E[X],
KZ′′​(0)=KN′′​(0)(KX′​(0))2+KN′​(0)KX′′​(0)=Var(N)(E[X])2+E[N]Var(X).

These are exactly E[Z] and Var(Z) from L12.

Worked example (Bertsekas Ex. 4.35): a geometric number of exponentials is exponential. Jane visits bookstores until she finds a book. Each store has it with probability p, and she spends an Exp(λ) time in each store. Total time Z=X1​+⋯+XN​ with N∼ Geometric(p). Then

MN​(s)=1−(1−p)espes​  es→λ−tλ​ ​ MZ​(t)=1−(1−p)λ−tλ​pλ−tλ​​=(λ−t)−(1−p)λpλ​=pλ−tpλ​.

So Z∼ Exp(pλ). This is surprising, since a sum of a fixed number n≥2 of exponentials is not exponential. Check the mean: E[Z]=E[N]E[X]=p1​⋅λ1​=pλ1​. ✓

Worked example (Bertsekas Problem 45): Poisson thinning. N∼ Poisson(λ) customers arrive, and each buys with probability p independently, so Xi​∼ Bernoulli(p). Then MN​(s)=eλ(es−1). Replace es by 1−p+pet:

MZ​(t)=eλ(1−p+pet−1)=eλp(et−1),

so the number of buyers is Poisson(λp).

Part B: extra worked examples and problems

B1 (Bertsekas Ex. 4.22, 4.27). P(X=2)=21​, P(X=3)=61​, P(X=5)=31​. Find MX​, E[X], E[X2], Var(X).

Solution

Solution. M(t)=21​e2t+61​e3t+31​e5t. Then M′(t)=e2t+21​e3t+35​e5t and M′′(t)=2e2t+23​e3t+325​e5t. So

E[X]=1+21​+35​=619​,E[X2]=2+23​+325​=671​,Var(X)=671​−36361​=3665​.

B2 (Bertsekas Problem 29). P(X=1)=21​, P(X=2)=P(X=3)=41​. Use the MGF to get E[X],E[X2],E[X3].

Solution

Solution. M(t)=21​et+41​e2t+41​e3t, and M(r)(0)=21​⋅1r+41​⋅2r+41​⋅3r:

E[X]=21​+42​+43​=47​,E[X2]=21​+1+49​=415​,E[X3]=21​+2+427​=437​.

B3 (Bertsekas Problem 32: spot the fake MGF). A non-negative integer-valued X has one of these as its MGF: (1) M(s)=e2(ees−1−1); (2) M(s)=e2(ees−1). (a) Which is impossible? (b) Find P(X=0).

Solution

Solution. (a) Every MGF has M(0)=1. For (1): M(0)=e2(e0−1)=e0=1. ✓ For (2): M(0)=e2(e−1)=1, so (2) is impossible. (b) For a non-negative integer variable, M(s)=∑k≥0​P(X=k)esk. As s→−∞, every term with k≥1 vanishes, so P(X=0)=lims→−∞​M(s) (Bertsekas Problem 38). Here es→0, so

P(X=0)=e2(e−1−1)≈0.2825.

B4 (Bertsekas Problem 36). X∼ Bernoulli(31​), Y∼ Exp(2), Z∼ Poisson(3), all independent. Find the MGFs of (a) U=XY+(1−X)Z, (b) 2Z+3, (c) Y+Z.

Solution

Solution. (a) U=Y if X=1 (probability 31​) and U=Z if X=0. Condition on X (and use independence): MU​(t)=31​MY​(t)+32​MZ​(t)=31​⋅2−t2​+32​e3(et−1), for t<2. This is a mixture. (b) Linear rule: M2Z+3​(t)=e3tMZ​(2t)=e3te3(e2t−1). (c) Independent sum: MY+Z​(t)=2−t2​e3(et−1), for t<2.

B5 (last year's HW6 Q5). X∼ Exp(2) and Y∼ Bernoulli(0.5) independent, Z=X+Y. Find MZ​, then E[Z] and Var(Z) from it.

Solution

Solution. MZ​(t)=2−t2​⋅21+et​=2−t1+et​ for t<2. Use the log shortcut: K(t)=ln(1+et)−ln(2−t).

K′(t)=1+etet​+2−t1​⇒E[Z]=21​+21​=1,K′′(t)=(1+et)2et​+(2−t)21​⇒Var(Z)=41​+41​=21​.

(Check: Var(X)+Var(Y)=41​+41​. ✓)

B6 (last year's Quiz 2 Q1, an exam question). Z=X+U with X∼ Exp(λ) and U∼U(0,1) independent. Derive E[Z] and E[Z2] using MGFs (state the domain of t).

Solution

Solution. MX​(t)=λ−tλ​ for t<λ; MU​(t)=tet−1​ for t=0, with MU​(0)=1. So MZ​(t)=λ−tλ​⋅tet−1​ for t<λ. For U, expand tet−1​=1+2t​+6t2​+⋯, so MU′​(0)=21​ and MU′′​(0)=31​. For X: MX′​(0)=λ1​ and MX′′​(0)=λ22​. By the product rule,

E[Z]=MX′​(0)+MU′​(0)=λ1​+21​,E[Z2]=MX′′​(0)+2MX′​(0)MU′​(0)+MU′′​(0)=λ22​+λ1​+31​.

B7 (last year's Tutorial 6 Q8). MX​(t)=1−3t1​, MY​(t)=(1−3t)21​ for t<31​, with X,Y independent. Find E[(X+Y)2].

Solution

Solution. MX+Y​(t)=(1−3t)−3. Then M′(t)=9(1−3t)−4 and M′′(t)=108(1−3t)−5, so E[(X+Y)2]=M′′(0)=108. (Check: X is exponential with mean 3 and variance 9; Y is Gamma with mean 6 and variance 18; so X+Y has mean 9 and variance 27, and 27+81=108. ✓)

B8 (Bertsekas Problem 34: inverting a product). Three penalty takers succeed independently with probabilities p1​,p2​,p3​. Find the pmf of the number of goals X from its MGF.

Solution

Solution. X is a sum of independent Bernoullis, so MX​(t)=∏i=13​(1−pi​+pi​et). Expand and read off the coefficient of ekt:

P(X=0)=(1−p1​)(1−p2​)(1−p3​),P(X=3)=p1​p2​p3​,
P(X=1)=p1​(1−p2​)(1−p3​)+(1−p1​)p2​(1−p3​)+(1−p1​)(1−p2​)p3​,
P(X=2)=p1​p2​(1−p3​)+p1​(1−p2​)p3​+(1−p1​)p2​p3​.

B9 (Bertsekas Ex. 4.34: random sum). A village has 3 gas stations, each open with probability 21​ independently. An open station has X∼U[0,1000] gallons. Find the MGF and the mean of the total available gas Y.

Solution

Solution. N∼ Binomial(3,21​), so MN​(s)=(21+es​)3. MX​(t)=1000te1000t−1​. Replace es by MX​(t):

MY​(t)=81​(1+1000te1000t−1​)3,E[Y]=E[N]E[X]=1.5×500=750 gallons.

B10 (Bertsekas Problem 42). Show that a random sum of independent normals need not be normal.

Solution

Solution. Let N be 1 or 2 with probability 21​ each, and Xi​∼N(0,1). Then MY​(t)=21​et2/2+21​et2. This is a mixture of N(0,1) and N(0,2). It is not of the form eμt+σ2t2/2, so by uniqueness Y is not normal.

B11 (Bertsekas Ex. 4.36). N∼ Geometric(p) and Xi​∼ Geometric(q), all independent. Show Y=X1​+⋯+XN​∼ Geometric(pq).

Solution

Solution. Replace es in MN​(s)=1−(1−p)espes​ by MX​(t)=1−(1−q)etqet​ and clear the inner denominator:

MY​(t)=1−(1−q)et−(1−p)qetpqet​=1−(1−pq)etpqet​,

which is the Geometric(pq) MGF.

B12 (Bertsekas Problem 43, exam style). A motorist meets 4 lights, each red with probability 21​ independently. Each red light costs an N(1,41​) wait (minutes), independently. Let X be the total wait. Find MX​ and P(X>4). Is X normal?

Solution

Solution. N∼ Binomial(4,21​) red lights, so MN​(s)=(21+es​)4, and each wait has MW​(t)=et+t2/8. Therefore

MX​(t)=(21+et+t2/8​)4.

Given N=n≥1, X∼N(n,n/4) (a sum of independent normals); given N=0, X=0. By total probability:

P(X>4)=n=1∑4​(n4​)161​[1−Φ(n/4​4−n​)]=164​(1−Φ(6))+166​(1−Φ(2.83))+164​(1−Φ(1.15))+161​(0.5)≈0.063.

X is not normal: it has an atom P(X=0)=161​.

B13 (probabilitycourse 6.1.6 Problems 8 and 9; last year's Tutorial 6 Q4). The engine of the LLN and the CLT. Let MX​ be finite near 0. Show

(a) n→∞lim​[MX​(ns​)]n=esE[X],(b) if E[X]=0, Var(X)=1: n→∞lim​[MX​(n​s​)]n=es2/2.
Solution

Solution. Near 0, Taylor's theorem gives MX​(u)=1+uE[X]+2u2​E[X2]+o(u2). (a) With u=s/n: MX​(s/n)=1+nsE[X]​+o(n1​), and (1+na​+o(n1​))n→ea, so the limit is esE[X]. (b) With u=s/n​, E[X]=0 and E[X2]=1: MX​(s/n​)=1+2ns2​+o(n1​), so the limit is es2/2.

Why this matters. [MX​(s/n)]n is the MGF of the sample mean nSn​​, and (a) says it tends to the MGF of the constant E[X] (a law of large numbers). [MX​(s/n​)]n is the MGF of n​Sn​​, and (b) says it tends to the MGF of N(0,1). That is the central limit theorem (L18). The normal MGF in (c) of the tutorial question is exactly es2/2.
